title: The Trade Credit Lerner Index

detail.title: The Trade Credit Lerner Index

declarations.declarationOfInterest: I have no conflict of interest to disclose
declarations.funderStatement: The study received no direct funding.

detail.abstract: A supplier and a buyer bargain jointly over prices and payment terms. The negotiated price is the Trade Credit Lerner Index (TCLI), the product of three components: the marginal cost, the markup, and the compounding factor at the supplier's adjusted cost of funds. At the reference parameterization, the Lerner Index overstates the true markup by 0.79% over a thirty-day payment term, and by up to 16% at longer payment terms and high adjusted costs of funds. Correcting the index for trade credit requires only the supplier's adjusted cost of funds over the payment term, with no demand elasticity or bargaining weight. With flexible prices, the two firms set the payment term where their joint financing surplus is largest, while the price divides the gains from the exchange. All benchmark results are closed form at a given bargaining weight. The firm financing the transaction depends on the two borrowing rates and the expected loss on the receivable. Firms use payment terms to extract rents when prices are sticky and managing receivables incurs variable costs. A buyer without an alternative supplier pays 3.75% more for the same good on identical payment terms.

detail.abstract:
Three earlier preregistered tests could not directly measure whether stock-market wealth transmits monetary policy to consumption less than housing wealth: the implied difference was far below what could be detected. This paper changes strategy. It combines marginal propensities to consume by wealth category (Beach, Gamber and Moran, 2025), responses of stock and house prices to the same high-frequency monetary-surprise factors (Swanson, 2021; Gorea, Kryvtsov and Kudlyak, 2024), and the observed composition of U.S. household wealth to quantify, under preregistered assumptions, how much consumption the asset revaluation triggered by a monetary surprise generates, and how this has changed since 1989. In the preregistered main specification, for forward guidance and asset purchases, the shift of wealth toward equities reduced the revaluation channel by 33% to 40% relative to the 1989 composition. In levels the channel is small, 2.7 to 4.0 basis points of annual consumption per standard deviation of the factor, and at point values the growth of wealth relative to consumption more than offset the composition effect. A non-preregistered sensitivity analysis with a January 2026 revision of the house-price responses confirms the asset-purchase result but weakens the forward-guidance one. The implied county-level difference sought by the previous test is 0.3% to 9% of its minimum detectable effect.

detail.abstract: This article proposes an original hypothesis concerning the competition of logos as geometric forms for attention and trust. The affective salience of a referent is hypothesized to confer an advantage on an associated sign already at its first independent test presentation following a fixed association-formation procedure; iconic signs without training are tested separately. The persistence of this advantage across repetitions and the possibility that a competing sign may offset it constitute separate testable predictions, not consequences of asymptotes specified for illustrative purposes. The transfer of evaluation from "referent → sign" is distinguished from the contextual effect of "sign → human bearer." A baseline model of trust dynamics, independent indicators of attention and direct competitive choice, and a program of empirical testing are presented. Numerical curves and ROC/AUC are illustrative; no experimental data are presented.

detail.abstract:
Privacy in retail central bank digital currencies (CBDCs) is usually framed as whether the central bank can identify the parties to a payment. This paper argues that a structurally different question matters as much: what information must be available to exercise monetary control. Where the classical account/token distinction asks what must be verified before a payment is accepted, we ask what state the validating component must hold, along two axes: the object of control, a subject’s monetary state or the individual monetary object, and the locus of acceptance, remote infrastructure or the parties to the payment, together with the locus at which misuse can be detected.

The framework separates four non-equivalent privacy properties and eight analytical dimensions. It is applied to the digital euro, including holding limits, offline payments and the funding and defunding lifecycle, and to three further designs spanning the account/token and online/offline divides. Account-based offline designs, for example, owe their payment privacy to local acceptance and cryptographic hiding of state rather than to the object of control. Tokenisation does not by itself produce anonymity, but a token-scoped design can confine re-identification to an incident-triggered, quorum-gated procedure that covers one token rather than a person’s financial history.

Two propositions result. Object-centric control does not remove monetary state from the control path but re-indexes it from holder to object, trading holder linkability for object linkability. A per-person holding limit presupposes binding a subject’s devices to that subject at registration; cryptography can hide the aggregate but not remove the binding, and across simultaneously offline devices that do not coordinate, the limit is guaranteed in real time only if it is pre-allocated among them.

The central proposition is therefore that the object of monetary control and the locus of acceptance jointly shape the privacy boundary, while the locus of detection constrains what can be established after a component is compromised; none of them, alone or together, is sufficient for anonymity. The design question is not only who may observe monetary information, but what the architecture requires anyone to know in order to control the money.

detail.abstract: Universal writing screening requires assessments that are both valid and feasible for school use. This study evaluated whether general-purpose artificial intelligence (AI) could automate comparative judgment (CJ) of student writing for screening. Specifically, the study examined agreement between ChatGPT-generated and human CJ scores, the extent to which ChatGPT-generated CJ scores (ChatGPT-CJ) predicted performance on standardized writing assessments, and whether these relations differed between emerging bilingual (EB) and non-EB students. ChatGPT-CJ scores were also compared with feature-based automated scoring systems and curriculum-based writing measures. Participants were 237 students in Grades 3-5 (n = 134 EB students, 57%) from five elementary schools in the southwestern United States. Students completed three writing screening tasks scored using human CJ, ChatGPT-CJ, writeAlizer, Project Essay Grade (PEG), and Correct Minus Incorrect Word Sequences (CIWS). Standardized writing assessments served as criterion measures. Agreement between human and ChatGPT judgments of identical writing pairs ranged from 76% to 81% (κ = .51-.61). ChatGPT-CJ scores were strongly associated with human CJ scores (r = .91-.92) and criterion writing quality (β = .96-.97). Relative to other scoring methods, ChatGPT-CJ scores demonstrated performance comparable to or stronger than human CJs, writeAlizer, PEG, and CIWS. No statistically significant differences in criterion validity were observed between EB and non-EB students. No practical differences were observed between ChatGPT models with reasoning enabled vs. disabled. Findings suggest general-purpose AI can generate writing quality scores that closely align with human judgments and provide valid indicators for universal screening.

detail.abstract: Ethereum's transition to Proof-of-Stake raised unresolved questions about whether its consensus mechanism could function as a market mechanism. This qualitative abductive study offers a technological, organisational and economic analysis through conceptual and document analysis. While Proof-of-Stake alone doesn't meet the criteria verbatim, its broader Ethereum ecosystem behaves similarly to a multi-layered market mechanism, even though a new class of intermediaries specialised in pool and double-staking could on the long run weaken this analogy.

detail.abstract: When the business cycles of many economies line up, a shock common to all of them stops cancelling in world output. We measure that alignment for 31 economies over 1970–2022, treating each economy’s 2–9 year cycle in real GDP per capita as a phase oscillator, and relate it to the five global recessions. Synchronization and swing size move together (detrended correlation +0.646). In recessions co-movement supplies 84.3% of the extra variance of world output, with correlation and larger swings contributing about equally: the 31 economies behave like about 3.5 independent ones on average and like one in 2020. Their correlation network has tightened 1.6× since the 1980s. With phases from past data only, synchronization is higher in the year before recessions (𝑝 = 0.038), but this rests on two events, 2009 and 2020. The variance of synchronization rises before recessions without its autocorrelation rising, so there is no critical slowing down; as an interpretation, this fits noise-induced rather than bifurcation-induced tipping. Simulated worlds with known coupling show which tests can be trusted. We make no forecasts.

detail.abstract: Petroleum consumption ARDL bound testing Nigeria Petroleum products remain the main fuels for transport, private electricity generation, and household use in Nigeria, yet the joint influence of regulated pump prices and renewable energy on their consumption has received little empirical attention. This study examines how the regulated pump price of petrol, used as a proxy for subsidy exposure, and renewable energy consumption affect the consumption of petroleum products in Nigeria from 1980 to 2021, with crude oil prices, output, and inflation as controls. An autoregressive distributed lag model is estimated within the bounds testing framework, and the selected specification is ARDL(1,0,1,0,0,0). The bounds test supports a long run relationship at the 5 percent level. In the long run, crude oil prices reduce consumption, whereas the pump price, renewable energy consumption, and output show positive associations. In the short run, a higher pump price lowers consumption, and an error correction term of-0.719 shows that about 72 percent of any disequilibrium is removed within a year. Diagnostic tests reveal no serial correlation, heteroskedasticity, or misspecification, although a level shift in 2013 calls for caution. Price reform restrains fuel demand mainly in the short run, and the renewable energy currently used in Nigeria does not displace petroleum products.

detail.abstract: Three things changed in 2026. On April 13, the fee to renounce U.S. citizenship fell from $2,350 to $450. On June 30, the Supreme Court held in Trump v. Barbara that a child born in the United States is a citizen at birth, whatever the parents' status, so an accidental American's tax duties begin at birth. And the IRS's quarterly list of people who expatriated kept growing. This manual follows two composite clients — Claire (born in Boston, raised in France) and Helen (a Canadian with a childhood green card) — from the first bank letter to a clean exit, covering renunciation, Form I-407 abandonment of residence, the Relief Procedures and Streamlined Filing Compliance Procedures, and the Form 8854 five-year certification that decides covered-expatriate status and the exit tax under section 877A. Appendices include completed pro forma filings and model FOIA requests. Published in the Journal of Tax Controversy (October 2026).

detail.abstract: The incorporation of social responsibility criteria into the selection of investment fund portfolios has gained prominence within financial, academic, and business circles, and its potential as a driver of transformation in corporate management is increasingly being recognized. The objective of this article is to identify key developments in the field of Socially Responsible Investment (SRI), specifically those concerning the selection of investment portfolios through the application of Multi-Criteria Decision-Making techniques and fuzzy logic. This paper presents a literature review on the characteristics of socially responsible portfolios and analyzes the motivations of socially responsible investors, seeking to understand and explain the decision-making process of this group of investors.

title: Strong-Copenhagen Stackelberg Games: Equilibrium as Contingent Emergence under Type Indeterminacy

detail.title: Strong-Copenhagen Stackelberg Games: Equilibrium as Contingent Emergence under Type Indeterminacy

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.

declarations.funderStatement: None.

detail.abstract: We propose an ontological framework for Stackelberg games under type indeterminacy. Departing from the standard Bayesian and behavioral game theory traditionsboth committed to an epistemic uncertainty paradigm where follower types are pre-existing properties to be inferredwe adopt a strong-Copenhagen ontological commitment: types do not exist as determinate properties prior to interaction, but are constituted through observation history. The framework treats strategies as acts-of-engagement rather than selections from pre-specied strategy sets, and treats payos as history-indexed emergent facts rather than ex-ante dened functions. We develop a multi-chain CPTP framework for the leader's belief about follower types, identify four cases of equilibrium structure (Nash equilibrium in both strategy and payo; payo equilibrium with strategy underdetermination; strategy equilibrium with payo nonequilibrium; neither), and characterize the conditions under which each case obtains. Nash equilibrium is recovered as a long-run limiting case under specic structural conditions. The framework provides testable predictions distinguishing it from epistemic frameworks: deployment-dependence of equilibrium structure, systematic Nash deviation in rst-time interactions, and ex-post discovered strategy underdetermination on payo-equivalent manifolds. Eight major existing frameworks (conjectural Stackelberg, behavioral game theory, Bayesian POMDP, quantum game theory, misspecied learning, robust Stackelberg, Markov perfect Stackelberg, strategic deception) are shown to share a common epistemic-uncertainty commitment that structurally precludes them from addressing these phenomena. Nonepistemic ontological alternatives (notably Bohmian pilot-wave; Haven 2005) are discussed in Section 3.1 as routes that could in principle support similar mathematical machinery through dierent commitments.

detail.abstract: Asset returns comove through global factors shared by all assets and local factors confined to a single industry, country, or asset class. The mapping from characteristics to factor exposures can also differ across these groups. We propose a conditional group factor model in which exposures to global and local factors are linear in characteristics, with a separate loading mapping for each group. We develop a five-stage procedure that estimates the global factors, the local factors, and their loading mappings. We derive convergence rates for estimators in every stages, establish consistency of within-group factor-number selection, and establish asymptotic normality for the estimated final factors and the final loading mapping matrices. Simulations show large gains over a pooled conditional factor model when the data have a group structure. In an application to a large panel of international stocks grouped by GICS sector, we identify a single global factor alongside sector-specific local factors, with sectors loading on the global factor through different characteristics. Outof-sample predictive R-squared reaches 0.71%, compared with at most 0.59% for pooled and group factor alternatives.

detail.abstract:
Background: Sparse and irregular longitudinal measurements make axial length (AL) growth difficult to predict after paediatric lens surgery. We aimed to develop and validate an observation-level, multi-horizon framework for individualised postoperative AL prediction in congenital ectopia lentis.

Methods: Of 437 patients in an initial multicentre retrospective cohort, 346 patients (612 eyes) contributed eligible observations for model development. The framework combined numeric gradient boosting with a multimodal neural network incorporating clinical text and ophthalmic images. It predicted AL at postoperative horizons from 0.5 to 5.0 years without imputing unobserved outcomes. We assessed performance using patient-grouped five-fold cross-validation and prospective temporal validation with 256 follow-up observations from 148 patients.

Findings: Patient-grouped five-fold cross-validation yielded a mean absolute error of 0.588 mm. Prospective temporal validation yielded an R² of 0.859, with performance similar to numeric gradient boosting alone. Numeric variables provided most of the predictive information; clinical text added modest value, whereas imaging offered limited improvement.

Interpretation: The framework supported individualised postoperative AL prediction from sparse and irregular longitudinal measurements. The similar performance of numeric gradient boosting alone suggests that numeric clinical variables accounted for most of the predictive value. These findings support further evaluation of individualised AL prediction for postoperative management.

detail.abstract: We study whether the early adoption of information technologies provides competitive advantages, and the source of these advantages. Existing research in this area has failed to differentiate between advantages that arise from the timing of adoption (e.g., asset preemption) and those that are related to higher levels of adoption (e.g., organizational learning). In this paper, we break down these advantages into two components: order of adoption (early vs. late adopters) and level of adoption (high vs. low internal diffusion levels). The empirical analysis examines the adoption and subsequent intrafirm diffusion of the automated teller machine in a sample of Spanish savings banks, using a long data panel, from 1988 to 2004. The results show that advantages associated to the order of adoption outweigh those associated to the level of adoption, and they have the potential to be long lasting. Our findings are consistent across various estimation methods, and we assess different performance dimensions (ROA, income, and efficiency). Our modelling and findings have implications for managers and can be applied to the study of the early adoption of modern technologies.

detail.abstract: Technology has a federalism problem. There are an increasing number of technologies for which three things are true all at once. First, they are critical to national security and defense. Second, they are dual-use-meaning they have civilian and military applications. And third, their cutting edge can be sharpened only in the private commercial sector. This paper calls them National Security Technologies-and for good reason. The Constitution places our national defense squarely in the hands of the federal government. And yet when it comes to NSTs, states make de facto national-defense decisions by passing legislation affecting the growth and trajectory of these technologies. For serious constitutional and normative reasons, this must stop. This paper explains why and how.

detail.abstract: Conspiracy narratives can emerge suddenly and spread widely on social media, carrying misinformation that erodes platforms' information environment. The resulting shifts of public attention, which we term conspiracy attention shocks, confront creators with a dilemma: false claims may attract new viewers but alienate existing followers, while restraint may cede them to competitors. Prior research focuses on how audiences respond to misinformation; how creators navigate this dilemma, and with what consequences, remains unclear. Drawing on attention economy theory, we examine how such shocks affect creators' misinformation production and net follower growth, and how audience size and attention practices shape these effects. We study the surge of the "kill line" narrative about American poverty on a leading Chinese video platform, combining propensity score matching with difference-indifferences. The shock increases misinformation production, including in videos unrelated to the narrative. Its null average effect on follower growth masks an asymmetry: smaller creators increase misinformation and gain followers, whereas larger creators do not significantly increase misinformation yet lose followers. Misinformation rises more among creators who frequently solicit engagement and less among those with commercial ties, and prior replies to core followers mitigate larger creators' follower losses. Robustness checks support these results. These findings identify conspiracy attention shocks as a driver of misinformation supply and extend attention economy theory: when attention moves, a large following offers no protection.

detail.abstract: Organizations frequently use Customer Care, Customer Assistance, Customer Service and Customer Support as if they were interchangeable. This paper argues that these functions have distinguishable operational perimeters and should not be collapsed into one generic category. Customer Care involves actions that look after the customer's well-being and experience, such as welcoming a hotel guest, checking whether an inconvenience has occurred, acknowledging a service incident or providing relevant recognition. Customer Assistance explains, guides and clarifies. Customer Service executes and delivers the requested or promised service at the point of transaction. Customer Support investigates, maintains, repairs, restores or resolves problems involving a product or service already provided. The paper examines how AI assistants may contribute to these functions across industries. It distinguishes four assistant roles: Consultative, Collaborative, Productive and Supportive. These roles describe primary purposes rather than mutually exclusive technologies or fixed levels of autonomy. Their suitability depends on the task, audience, permissions, restrictions, expected behavior and demonstrable value to both the organization and its customers. Security, access control, traceability and human accountability are cross-cutting requirements. The paper argues that over-engineering, misuse, poor task fit and underuse can increase effort, risk and customer dissatisfaction rather than improve outcomes. AI should therefore be selected and evaluated against the requirements and outcomes of the customer function it supports.

detail.abstract:
Extended producer responsibility (EPR) for packaging is spreading quickly across low- and middle-income countries, and governments increasingly present it as a tool to prevent plastic waste. Reusable packaging can prevent waste when containers return often enough, yet EPR schemes were built to finance collection and recycling. I ask whether and how EPR can finance reuse systems in developing countries. I combine a scoping review of 143 peer-reviewed and grey sources with a document analysis of packaging EPR instruments in Indonesia, India, the Philippines, Vietnam, Chile, Kenya and South Africa, benchmarked against the European Union. Only 14 sources examine reuse together with EPR or deposit-refund systems, none of them on financing reuse in a developing country, and only two study reuse systems empirically in developing countries. Across the instruments, reusable packaging is mostly exempted, deducted or credited. Reuse lowers what producers owe, but only South Africa explicitly allows scheme revenue to be spent on reuse, and no instrument in the sample modulates fees on reusability. I identify five design tensions between EPR and reuse, concerning the unit of obligation, metrics, fee modulation, eligible use of funds and recognised actors. A stylised fee model shows that charging reusable packaging by weight penalises reuse until return rates are high, while exemption removes any fee-based reward for raising them. I propose charging producers only for containers lost from a verified reuse system, ring-fencing revenue for shared infrastructure and paying neighbourhood retailers as return points, and I set out five testable propositions.

detail.abstract: Layla, a senior manager, keeps a private notebook of what her engagements are not looking at: forty-seven documents of observations the scope did not ask for and the firm has no place to put. This paper starts from her case. A consulting firm that codifies its methods and runs them through governed AI agents gains consistency and provenance. It also loses the conditions that produce new methods, until its playbook becomes something the client's own team can run with the same models. The paper proposes a second architecture that sits beside delivery governance, with its own funding and its own rules. Its parts include reading the reviewer dissent record for methodology signal; an observation channel for staff below the senior tier; a methodology development career track; an innovation scope that covers products, services, AI training feedback, and technology investment; and incentives that reward divergence without inviting gaming. A written conflict rule says exploration wins when it clashes with delivery efficiency. A rotating Red Team and an Innovation Reserve of 2 to 3 percent of practice revenue back it. Cultural calibration for high power-distance markets runs through the design.

detail.title: Value-Native AI: Infrastructure for Creating, Identifying, and Capturing Value in the Age of AI

detail.abstract: The world is making the largest concentrated capital bet of our lifetimes on artificial intelligence: more than $750 billion in 2026 capital spending by four technology companies alone, and $2.7 trillion in forecast worldwide AI spending. Yet 56 percent of chief executives report no significant financial benefit from AI to date. Whether this investment produces real economic value, and who captures it, is the central economic question of the AI era. We are measuring the wrong thing. Investment in AI is tracked in seats, licenses, and utilization by organizations, and in tools tried and hours spent by individuals, none of which is denominated in anything a CFO, a funder, a public budget, or a career actually counts. The result is motion without return: the tool becomes the anchor, and value is left to appear as a byproduct. It does not appear, because value has never been a byproduct. This paper introduces Value-Native AI, an approach in which value creation, not AI adoption, is the organizing principle, and presents a framework for maximizing the return on AI, for any individual and any organization. It has three co-equal pillars: four human capabilities (augmentation, orchestration, synthesis, and translation) operating on a substrate of judgment; six forms of economic value, held to three credibility disciplines (pre-registered baselines, evidence held in systems of record, and attestation); and eight forms of capture available to professionals and organizations. Because every organization, and every working person, exists to create value and differs only in the currency counted, the framework functions as a shared substrate across firms, nonprofits, research institutions, public agencies, and the individual career. The framework also resolves a puzzle the industry has misdiagnosed. Slow workforce adoption is largely rational behavior under missing reward infrastructure rather than a skills deficit, which makes it an organizational design problem rather than a training one. Drawing on field experience training more than four hundred professionals through the Greenwood AI Center of Excellence, a federally designated Tech Hub initiative, and on the empirical literature, the paper states a falsifiable prediction: matched organizations sorted by whether their primary AI metric is an outcome denomination or a utilization metric will diverge on sustained adoption and realized returns within twenty-four months.

detail.abstract: Most technology adoption research treats adoption as the outcome that matters, on the assumption that people who adopt a technology will go on to use it. This paper tests that assumption. Building on the pro-poor "context, community and culture" perspective (Potnis, 2014), we propose a three-stage model in which contextual factors make a technology reachable, community and cultural factors influence whether people start using it, and a separate set of factors decides whether they keep using it. We test the model with partial least squares structural equation modelling on survey data from 385 low-income adults in three informal settlements in Nairobi, Kenya, using mobile financial services. The model explains 66.2% of the variance in adoption and 48.9% in continued usage. Context, community and culture all influence adoption, with community factors, and effort expectancy within them, the strongest. Continued usage, however, follows a different pattern: contextual factors have the strongest effect, community factors remain significant, cultural factors have no significant effect, and adoption itself does not predict usage. Age and gender neither influence adoption and usage directly nor moderate the relationships tested. The findings suggest that adoption and continued use are distinct outcomes with distinct causes, and that research and practice which measure adoption alone may overstate the success of a technology. We discuss implications for adoption theory and for organisations introducing new technologies, including artificial intelligence.

detail.abstract: Housing is the largest asset for most U.S. households and a primary source of climate risk exposure. This review synthesizes a rapidly growing empirical literature at the intersection of homeowners insurance, housing markets, and climate risk, emphasizing recent work using newly available granular insurance data. We organize the discussion around three questions: how much risk households retain, how insurance premiums are determined, and how disruptions in insurance markets create public sector exposures. Despite widespread insurance take-up, substantial household wealth remains unprotected. Insurance pricing, shaped by growing expected losses and state regulation, influences coverage gaps, property values, mortgage credit, and incentives for location choice and adaptation. Disruptions in insurance coverage also shift losses toward public backstops, linking insurance market outcomes to broader fiscal exposures. We identify open questions about how insurance market design and public policy can balance household financial protection, incentives for risk reduction, and fiscal exposure.

title: PAPER 06 - Machine-Speed Economics: How Evidence Becomes the Price Signal

detail.title: PAPER 06 - Machine-Speed Economics: How Evidence Becomes the Price Signal

declarations.funderStatement: Self-funded. No external funding was received for this work.

detail.abstract:
An economy is buyers meeting sellers, prices moving, and obligations settling — with enough reliability that strangers will trade. This paper describes that economy with the humans removed from the middle of each transaction, and argues that what makes it possible is not faster money but independently witnessed evidence.

The paper makes six claims. First, the machine-speed economy requires nothing that does not already exist. Agents carry a purse — bounded spending authority committable at the point of action — and a mandate — preconstrained limits on what may be done, for whom, at what cost. Every component maps to deployed technology. The assembly is connection, not invention.

Second, admissibility becomes the matching criterion. Today, matching happens first, and humans check compliance afterward, usually too late. Where two agents' constraint sets intersect, a trade is admissible; where they do not, no candidate ever appears. There is no non-compliant transaction to prevent because it was never matchable.

Third, once parties attest to latency, uptime, jurisdiction, security posture, and energy mix, those attestations become bid attributes. Price discovery turns real-world differences into numerical differences. The market prices pickiness, which no human market can sustain, because no human holds the whole vector.

Fourth, a receipt is not a payment. Execution, evidence, obligation, settlement, and enforcement are five distinct functions, and collapsing any two destroys the unpaid state — the economy's ability to say the service occurred, the obligation exists, the payment has not cleared. An architecture that fires a payment per action has nothing to net.

Fifth, and this is the paper's candidate for what is new: a single evidence artifact does three jobs at once. The receipt that proves a determination was legitimate is the IOU the settlement layer nets and the input the valuation layer prices on. Governance control, settlement primitive, valuation denominator — one artifact, three functions, each reinforcing the others. No prior literature appears to synthesize them.

Sixth, the thesis is falsifiable by a single measurement. Run the same market governed and ungoverned and compare prices. If the spread is zero — if nobody will pay for attested terms, deterministic admissibility, and independent evidence — the thesis is wrong. Not incomplete. Wrong.

detail.abstract: Policy analysis of mineral and fuel economies requires timely, comparable and reproducible dependence measures, whereas existing measures trade conceptual breadth against coverage. The Extractives Dependence Index ends in 2011, the Mining Contribution Index covers 110 economies in 2022, and the World Bank resource-rent series ends in 2021. This article introduces the Natural Resource Dependence Index (NRDI), which combines the resource share of merchandise exports with resource exports relative to GDP. Built on harmonised trade and GDP data, it covers up to 205 economies annually over 1995-2025; the same algorithm yields mineral and fuel modules, and an agricultural module completes the aggregate. The mineral module tracks the Mining Contribution Index (ρ = 0.85) and the fuel module the Extractives Dependence Index (ρ = 0.74), with negative cross-domain correlations. A criterion-validity test of a pre-specified hypothesis associates higher lagged dependence with a stronger two-year growth response to global commodity-price shocks, although this aggregate association is borderline under year-clustered bootstrap inference. The NRDI adds information beyond mineral rents and, under the pre-specified inference, beyond export specialisation; however, the criterion does not distinguish it from total resource rents or extractive export shares, and no measure shows a detectable out-of-sample predictive advantage. Higher fuel dependence is associated with a stronger response to energy-price shocks, whereas no two-year response to metal-price shocks is detectable for the mineral module; shock sensitivity should not be assumed homogeneous across resource classes. The article's contribution lies not in prediction but in a transparent, annually updatable architecture for measuring resource dependence and comparing mineral and fuel exporters on a common scale.

detail.abstract: Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) is simultaneously the least culpable for the climate problem and one of the most vulnerable to its repercussions. Despite these risks, SSA has enormous, untapped potential to contribute to global mitigation efforts thanks to its substantial natural capital-including the Congo Basin, the Sahel, and mangrove ecosystems-and significant renewable energy resources. The Paris Agreement's Article 6.2 mechanism provides an important opportunity for SSA countries to convert their mitigation potential into sustainable development financing, allowing SSA governments to monetize emission reductions from activities such as avoided deforestation, afforestation, agroforestry, clean cooking, and renewable energy deployment. In parallel, the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), which includes 54 nations and 1.4 billion people, provides a supplementary framework for incorporating climate-conscious industry into Africa's overall economic integration drive. AfCFTA may standardize carbon requirements, open up cross-border renewable energy markets, and encourage green value chains like sustainable cement, electric transportation, and regional solar corridors. It also paves the door for a continental carbon market architecture in which African goals, rather than global buyer interests, determine the terms of involvement. This article contends that SSA may use the synergies between Article 6.2 procedures and the AfCFTA's integration framework to accomplish a fair, sovereign, and inclusive energy transition. By incorporating climate financing into Africa's development strategy, the continent has the potential to not only strengthen resilience and cut emissions but also to pioneer a unique form of climate-conscious growth that is both equitable and internationally significant.

detail.abstract: Debates on federalism in the Philippines frequently emphasize regional autonomy, political representation, economic development, and the distribution of governmental power. However, changing the constitutional structure of government does not automatically resolve disparities in administrative capacity, fiscal resources, accountability, or public service delivery. This study examines Philippine federalism through a proposed Institutional Alignment Framework (IAF), which evaluates the relationship among institutional readiness, fiscal equity, democratic accountability, and national coordination and resilience. Using qualitative documentary analysis, the study examines constitutional and statutory provisions, official policy reports, and relevant scholarly literature on decentralization, fiscal federalism, and constitutional reform. The documentary synthesis indicates that the central policy question is not simply whether federalism is preferable to a unitary system, but whether the proposed allocation of authority would be supported by adequate resources, capable institutions, effective oversight, and workable intergovernmental arrangements. The Philippine Constitution already recognizes local autonomy, decentralization, local revenue powers, and a just share of national taxes, while the World Bank's assessment of the Mandanas ruling identifies persistent concerns involving fiscal disparities, implementation capacity, and coordination. These issues remain relevant to any proposal for deeper regional autonomy. The study proposes the IAF as a diagnostic framework for evaluating federal reform proposals and strengthening existing decentralization arrangements. It does not establish that federalism will necessarily produce better outcomes; instead, it identifies institutional conditions that should be assessed before major constitutional restructuring is undertaken.

detail.abstract: Gross domestic product (GDP) is a central measure of economic activity, but it does not independently capture an economy's productive capacity, international connectivity, resilience-related buffers, or selected structural capabilities. This paper presents the JAS Unified Economic Strength Index (JESI), a multidimensional composite framework designed to complement conventional macroeconomic indicators. JESI Master Version 1.0 combines five pillars-Growth, Productivity, Connectivity, Resilience, and Strategic Autonomy-using fixed weights of 0.20, 0.25, 0.20, 0.20, and 0.15, respectively. The pillars are aggregated through a weighted geometric formula. The empirical application covers Bangladesh, India, Indonesia, Malaysia, and Vietnam over 2016-2023. The theoretical panel contains 40 country-year observations, of which 34 are complete cases. Bangladesh contributes two complete observations, while each of the other four countries contributes eight. The reported baseline country means are highest for Malaysia (59.2828), followed by Vietnam (57.1607), India (48.6351), Indonesia (46.8245), and Bangladesh (34.4635). These results are descriptive and conditional on the available observations and the production specification. A Phase 3 normalization sensitivity audit compares the baseline with five alternatives. Full-sample min-max, winsorized min-max, and percentile specifications reconstruct scores from indicator inputs using alternative monotonic transformations. Two additional specifications change the reference bounds used for nonlinear scoring of government debt and the current-account balance while retaining the other pillars at their production baseline values. The results show that numerical score differences and ranking stability are distinct. Full-sample min-max changes the relative mean ranks of India and Indonesia, while the other four specifications preserve the baseline country-mean ordering. The P5-P95 Resilience reference-zone alternative produces the smallest reported score differences, although its scope is narrower than that of the three indicator-rescoring alternatives. A production reconciliation check reports zero displayed mean and maximum absolute differences between composite values reconstructed from persisted pillar scores and the corresponding persisted production values. This establishes consistency within the scope of that check, not independent end-to-end reproducibility from all original data sources. The audit also identifies zero-valued Growth scores under certain diagnostic alternatives, illustrating how normalization interacts with geometric aggregation. The paper concludes that JESI is a documented, empirically evaluated research framework, but the current evidence does not establish universal validity, predictive superiority, or complete independent reproducibility. Differences between production code and some methodological documentation, uneven panel coverage, and outstanding source-data provenance requirements should be addressed in subsequent research.

detail.abstract: The same policy often produces different outcomes in different societies, and the literature on external validity, state-dependent multipliers, culture, and path dependence documents this from different angles. What is missing is a unified account in which the policy environment is itself an object that policy changes. This paper develops a minimal dynamic model in which a social context (historical experience, norms, the economic environment, and expectations) shapes both the implementation and the behavioral response to a policy, while the policy in turn reshapes the context. Four results follow. (i) Policy effects coincide across contexts at every scale ⇔ two aggregate sufficient statistics coincide, and context matters for the effect only through its interaction with the policy; shifts in expectations or norms that move behavior in levels leave the effect unchanged. (ii) The sign of a policy's effect can reverse across contexts, and the dependence of the effect on context is logically distinct from the dependence of the optimal policy on context. (iii) Because policy changes the transition law of the context and, locally, its Jacobian, it can move a society across a stability boundary, making initial differences vanish or become amplified. (iv) With strategic complementarity in norms, a temporary policy has a permanent effect when its scale and duration place the intervention above a joint dose-duration frontier, and under crowding-out a policy can yield a gain on impact and a loss in discounted dynamic welfare. The results give testable restrictions and a precise sense in which evidence from one society transports to another.

detail.abstract: This treatise proposes and defines the foundational conceptual frameworks of "AI Transcendentalism" (AI 超验主义, or AI 超验) and "Silicon Transcendentalism" (硅基超验主义, or 硅基超验), establishing the technical-philosophical boundaries between computational state representation and biological intervention. As large language models and autonomous agents assume an expanding share of decision-making in pharmaceutical research, modern R&D operates under an implicit technological faith: that continuous architectural scaling and tokenized biological data will automatically yield causal discoveries. Writing from Walden Pond, the historical center of New England Transcendentalism, the author argues that this ideology conflates state classification with dynamic transformation. Observational datasets (such as static single-cell transcriptomic profiles) teach a model the static "nouns" (cellular states) of biology, but fail to inherently resolve the transactional "verbs" (directional perturbations) that govern therapeutic outcomes. No amount of computational scaling substitutes for anchoring algorithmic hypotheses within complementary multi-modal matrices and empirical wet-lab validation. The essay extends this inquiry to clinical outcome prediction, where increasingly accurate forecasts of longitudinal disease trajectories and mortality risk remain safe only as long as an accurate forecast is not mistaken for a validated treatment-selection rule, and where even a correctly used forecast trades human narrative contingency for statistical certainty. The treatise concludes by outlining an Emersonian middle path of evidence-anchored technological practice, positioning Silicon Transcendentalism as a distinct modern philosophical inquiry into the boundaries of human and machine intelligence.

detail.abstract: Out-of-sample does not always mean out of sight. Researchers may keep future returns out of parameter estimation yet still use them to develop the prediction model. We quantify this informational advantage by comparing an ex-ante protocol, which selects among forecasting specifications using pre-test data, with an ex-post protocol, which makes this choice once the test sample becomes available. Across 36 equity markets and eight models, seeing the test sample nearly doubles Sharpe ratios. The gap is larger with broader design menus, smaller training samples, and higher idiosyncratic volatility. Out-of-sample performance can therefore reflect hindsight-not just forecasting skill.

detail.abstract: We measure the time horizon of U.S. presidential policy proposals using 2,748 proposals from every State of the Union address and annual message from 1946 to 2024, coded blind to the speaker and date. In a model where a president values long-run payoffs only if he expects to see them, older presidents propose shorter-horizon policies and the end of the re-election motive lengthens the horizon in a second term. In the pre-specified test, the horizon tilt of proposals falls by 0.57 standard deviations per decade of age, and age rather than political experience carries the effect. The estimate is stable across specifications, but with fourteen presidents its significance depends on the controls. Second-term proposals have longer horizons. A risk-taking channel finds no support, and growth stocks co-move with the horizon of proposals without reacting to the addresses themselves.

detail.abstract: This paper investigates the relationship between Airbnb short-term rental activity and residential rents in Quebec, Canada. Using cross-sectional microdata comprising approximately 5,000 Airbnb listings and 8,300 residential rental listings, we employ a hedonic pricing framework augmented with spatial econometric techniques to quantify the conditional association between nearby Airbnb presence and monthly rents. For each rental listing we construct Airbnb exposure measures within 250 m, 500 m, 1 km, and 2 km buffers using Haversine distances. Our baseline estimates indicate that an additional Airbnb listing within 500 m is associated with a statistically significant increase in monthly rent of approximately 0.3-0.5%, controlling for dwelling characteristics, building type, and city fixed effects. Quantile regressions reveal that this association is stronger at the upper tail of the rent distribution. A complementary hedonic model of Airbnb nightly prices indicates that short-term rental pricing is driven primarily by listing characteristics, with no significant premium attached to city-level rents. Robustness checks-including alternative buffer radii, subsample analyses, and machine-learning benchmarks-confirm the stability of the rent-exposure association. We discuss the policy implications of these results for housing affordability and short-term rental regulation, while cautioning that cross-sectional associations should not be interpreted as causal effects.

detail.abstract: We estimate a large-scale hedonic price model for the Canadian residential real-estate market using a cross-section of 140,931 active MLS listings drawn from the nine provinces present in the data. A semi-logarithmic specification decomposes dwelling prices into structural attributes, dwelling type and ownership form, and 1,153 neighbourhood (Forward Sortation Area) fixed effects estimated by absorbing least squares. Moving from a purely structural model to the full specification raises the explained share of price variation from 46% to 77%, establishing that location is the dominant price determinant in Canada: neighbourhood effects alone account for roughly thirty percentage points of explanatory power. The living-area elasticity is 0.51-0.62, each full bathroom commands a premium of about 11-15%, and-conditional on floor space-bedroom counts are economically negligible. The implicit prices are stable across alternative samples and trimming rules, and the model delivers strong out-of-sample valuation accuracy (held-out R 2 = 0.76; median absolute error of 16%). The neighbourhood effects absorb the bulk of the spatial dependence in prices-Moran's I falls from 0.46 to 0.08-and we further document diminishing returns to floor space, an urban price gradient that decays with distance to major metros, and quantile and cross-province heterogeneity in the implicit prices. We map the resulting neighbourhood premia, which span a factor of roughly nine between the most and least expensive areas.

detail.abstract: Supermarket promotions disproportionately target less healthy foods. Removing such promotions may reduce the purchases of these foods. In this study, we evaluated the impact of voluntary removal of volume price promotions in one major UK supermarket on household expenditure of soft drinks and confectionery products. We used household purchase data from the Worldpanel by Numerator UK consumer panel, encompassing approximately 30,000 households. We analysed this dataset using a difference-indifference methodology (two-way fixed-effects). We found that, following the removal of volume price promotions, households predominantly shopping at the intervention supermarket reduced their total expenditure on soft drinks and confectionery purchased by 4.7% (95% CI:-6.7% to-2.6%) and 3.9% (95% CI:-5.8% to-2.1%), respectively, relative to comparison households. Expenditure on soft drinks and confectionery products that were on volume price promotions decreased by 23.2% (95% CI:-17.4,-26.0) and 7.7% (95% CI:-2.3,-12.7), respectively. Concurrently, expenditure on products that were on temporary price reductions increased by 6.9% (95% CI: 4.2, 9.8) for soft drinks and 8.4% (95% CI: 6.2, 10.7) for confectionery. These results are similar for the quantity of soft drinks and confectionery purchased. Overall, our results suggest that removing volume price promotions can reduce total expenditure and volume of soft drinks and confectionery purchased, but to effectively reduce the overall purchases of less healthy foods, a ban on promotions may need to go beyond volume price promotions only.

detail.abstract:
Price elasticity of demand is a fundamental economic concept that explains the responsiveness of quantity demanded to changes in price. It is also an important tool for understanding how price changes affect total revenue. When a firm reduces the price of a commodity, the resulting increase in quantity demanded may or may not compensate for the reduction in price. Consequently, total revenue may decrease, remain unchanged, or increase depending on the responsiveness of demand. Although these relationships are well established in economic theory, integrating the graphical visualization of elasticity with the interpretation of revenue effects and the factors contributing to revenue change remains a relevant methodological objective.

This paper develops the Integrated Scale Efficiency Decomposition Method (ISEDM), a framework designed to integrate the visualization of price elasticity of demand with the interpretation of its associated revenue effects. The method seeks to present elasticity and revenue change as interconnected aspects of a price change rather than as separate concepts requiring independent analysis. Its graphical construction employs a deliberately specified relationship between the scales of the price and quantity axes. This normalization is central to the method because it establishes the intended correspondence between the graphical representation and the elasticity measure, enabling demand responsiveness to be interpreted visually within a consistent framework.

Beyond visualizing elasticity, ISEDM develops an integrated approach to interpreting changes in total revenue. It considers the revenue reduction associated with applying a lower price to the reference quantity and the additional revenue generated by the increase in quantity demanded at the lower price. Examining these components together provides a structured explanation of how a price reduction produces different revenue outcomes under different demand conditions. The framework also introduces a price-elasticity-of-revenue measure to express the revenue effect of a price reduction relative to the corresponding price-change benchmark.

A further contribution of the paper is the development of two complementary models. The Elasticity-Change Effect Model (or Efficiency Effect Model) which examines how revenue outcomes vary when demand responsiveness changes while the magnitude of the price change remains constant. The Price-Change Effect Model (or Scale Effect Model) which examines how revenue outcomes vary when the magnitude of the price change changes while demand responsiveness remains constant. Together, these models provide a systematic approach to examining the distinct roles of demand responsiveness and price-change magnitude in determining revenue outcomes.

The research gap addressed by this paper is methodological and integrative rather than the discovery of a previously unknown relationship between price elasticity and total revenue. While established economic principles explain the relationship between elasticity and revenue, ISEDM seeks to bring graphical visualization, revenue-effect interpretation, and the separate examination of elasticity-change and price-change effects into a unified framework. Through conceptual development, graphical constructions, and numerical illustrations, the paper presents ISEDM as an approach intended to improve the understanding and interpretation of price elasticity and its revenue implications. Its comparative analytical advantages, practical applicability, and pedagogical effectiveness remain subjects for further investigation.

The limitation of this model is that, it is applicable for any two points taken at a time on a downward sloping linear demand curve which represent the corresponding values of P and QD in number of units. Preferably, an upper left point on a download sloping linear demand curve as initial point which represents (OPN and OQL) and thereafter, any subsequent point will be either (OPL1 and OQN1) or (OPL2 and OQN2) or (OPL3 and OQN3) etc. as we move downward along the demand curve from left to right for graphical visualization of mathematical relationship between Ed, Er and change in TR.

Keywords: Price elasticity of demand; Integrated Scale Efficiency Decomposition Method (ISEDM); total revenue; revenue decomposition; graphical visualization; demand responsiveness; elasticity-change effect; price-change effect.

detail.abstract: I formalize free will through three choice axioms: reasons-responsive control, irreducible alternativism, and constructive sourcehood. For open systems, sourcehood implies alternativism; control is independent of both. A deliberately stochastic rule satisfies alternativism but admits a non-invasive classical extension, separating the two openness conditions. A quantum system with two binary contexts satisfies all three axioms and yields an explicit discrepancy between direct and sequenced probabilities. The separation concerns non-invasive representations; classical processes with state disturbance can also satisfy the axioms.

detail.abstract:
In an increasingly polarized nation, in which we no longer can reach any consensus about what is meant by the term “common good,” it might be wise to extend additional protections to national monuments from executive branch interference. But prior to doing so, the U.S. Congress may want to undertake some additional research work. Such research could build on the existing charge of the National Park Service as well as other interested parties. By doing so, Congress gains insight into whether and how this federal legislature should make greater use of the national historical parks designation.

This article explains, at least in part, how Congress could carry out such research and policy work in the wake of recent expansions in executive power. It does so by introducing a new national historical parks dataset. This dataset, which draws upon National Park Service (NPS) data about the sixty-three (63) existing national historical parks and how they are distributed across national space, may be used to undertake a range of useful analyses. One example of a case in point is a distributional analysis, which could explain how all 63 national historical parks are distributed across U.S. national space on the basis of race, income and population.

The article undertakes this type of distributional analysis in its four (II-V) additional parts. Part II describes the applicable federal law for national parks. Part III explains this article’s methodological approach. Part IV contains its analysis. Part V contains its conclusions and recommendation, as well as a potentially viable implementation plan.

detail.abstract: This paper asks whether Vietnam's expanding electronics production base became less dependent on concentrated import sources between 2015 and 2023. It constructs an audited annual UN Comtrade panel for telecommunications equipment (HS 8517) and integrated circuits (HS 8542), harmonizes six-digit subheadings into 11 stable product families, and combines partner concentration, geographic composition, exact HHI decompositions, and a fixed-product-basket counterfactual. The aggregate headings conceal sharply different trajectories. Communicationparts imports fell from US$20.78 billion in 2022 to US$5.85 billion in 2023; their HHI rose from 0.468 to 0.713 as the Republic of Korea's share fell from 55.9 to 6.5 percent. Holding 2015 product weights fixed attributes 95.6 percent of the aggregate HS 8517 concentration increase to within-family partner reallocation rather than product-mix change. Integrated-circuit processors expanded from US$3.14 billion to US$17.80 billion while their HHI declined from 0.265 to 0.143; memories instead became more concentrated, with the Republic of Korea supplying 68.5 percent in 2023. Aggregate IC diversification partly reflects the growing weight of the more diversified processor family. The findings show why heading-level concentration can misstate dependence and why customs-partner diversification should not be equated with operational resilience.

detail.abstract: Gold is increasingly represented, traded, transferred, and collateralised through digital infrastructure. Yet the language used to describe these processes often collapses several legally and operationally distinct states into the single term "settlement." Economic exposure to gold, a contractual claim denominated in gold, proprietary ownership of identified or pooled physical metal, transfer of title or beneficial interest, and final discharge of an underlying obligation are not equivalent events. This paper develops the Gold Settlement Finality Test, an analytical framework for determining what has actually become final when a gold-related transaction is said to have settled. The framework separates five states: economic exposure, contractual entitlement, proprietary ownership, legally effective transfer, and discharge of the underlying obligation. It then tests settlement architectures against the identity of the settlement asset, the nature of the rights transferred, the legal effectiveness and irrevocability of transfer, custody and intermediary dependencies, the treatment of failure, and the point at which the original obligation ceases to exist. The distinction is particularly important as the gold market moves beyond the traditional allocated and unallocated account structures of the Loco London market toward pooled ownership structures, tokenised gold, transferable digital interests, and shared infrastructure such as the World Gold Council's proposed Gold as a Service model. Digitalisation can reduce reconciliation costs, increase transferability, and improve operational efficiency. It does not, by itself, establish settlement finality. The paper argues that a transaction may be operationally complete at one layer while remaining legally or economically incomplete at another. A token may move without proprietary title moving; proprietary rights may move without extinguishing the underlying obligation; and an apparently final digital transfer may remain dependent upon an issuer, custodian, account provider, or external settlement mechanism. The Gold Settlement Finality Test therefore shifts the central question from whether a gold instrument is "backed," "allocated," or "digital" to a more demanding question: what precisely has been transferred, under whose authority, with what legal effect, and at what point can neither party legitimately claim that the original obligation remains unsettled? The framework is intended for application across physical bullion, allocated and unallocated accounts, pooled ownership structures, tokenised gold, and emerging physical-asset settlement architectures.

detail.abstract: A smartphone is commonly understood as a single commercial product owned, manufactured, and sold by a particular company. From the perspective of intellectual property rights (IPR), however, a smartphone represents a complex convergence of several distinct legal regimes. Copyright may protect its software, graphical user interface, and original artistic elements; trademark law may protect its brand name, logo, and source-identifying features; design law may protect its external appearance; patent law may protect qualifying technological inventions embodied in its hardware and software-related functionality; and trade secret law may protect confidential technical information, manufacturing processes, and commercially sensitive algorithms. Additional legal considerations arise where smartphones incorporate open-source software, third-party technologies, semiconductor layout-designs, or culturally significant designs and symbols. This article examines the intellectual property architecture of a smartphone under Indian law, drawing on the Copyright Act, 1957, the Trade Marks Act, 1999, the Designs Act, 2000, the Patents Act, 1970, and other relevant legal instruments. It considers the challenges created by technological convergence, artificial intelligence, software licensing, standard-essential patents, and complex supply chains. It argues that a smartphone should not be treated as a single, undifferentiated object of ownership but as a product containing multiple intellectual property assets, potentially controlled by different rights-holders. The article proposes a product-centred analytical framework, described as the product's intellectual property "X-ray", to identify the rights embedded in a smartphone and the legal consequences of its manufacture, distribution, marketing, repair, and use.

detail.abstract: Creator businesses sell, borrow against, and bequeath social media accounts that the platforms say cannot be sold, borrowed against, or bequeathed. This Article argues that the usual question, who owns the account, has no single answer because an account is five different things governed by five different bodies of law: a contract, a set of credentials, a body of copyrighted content, a name and persona, and an audience. It then makes four claims. First, followers are owned by no one, but the value they represent is goodwill, which corporate, tax, and contract law have allocated for more than a century. Second, courts should enforce private allocations of account value between the parties to a deal even where platform terms forbid transfer, leaving the platform its remedy of termination. Third, courts should recognize an account as a property-like interest good against everyone except the platform. Fourth, directors and officers of companies whose revenue rests on a platform account owe oversight duties to that dependency, and a board that has never asked who controls the credentials has not discharged them. A single $20 million hypothetical carries the analysis through account anatomy, allocation among claimants, sales, creator contracts, taxation, valuation, acquisitions, founder departures, board duties, AI-generated assets, digital inheritance, and reform.

detail.abstract: This paper investigates the planetary-scale ecological and biogeochemical risks associated with the potential creation of self-replicating chirally inverted (mirror) autotrophs or lithotrophs capable of growth on achiral substrates. Because these mirror organisms would be entirely removed from the stereospecific mortality terms (viral lysis and assimilatory grazing) that regulate the natural biosphere, we derive the exact competitive-exclusion condition showing they could displace natural primary producers despite a 5- to 20-fold handicap in maximum growth rate. We demonstrate that this takeover would replace the fast biological recycling of limiting elements with a slow geological one, bounding sustainable primary production to 0.26–1.0% of its natural value and establishing a quasi-absorbing state of collapse from which recovery would exceed collapse time by one to three orders of magnitude. Crucially, we prove that the condition for competitive exclusion is mathematically identical to the condition for a released founder population to establish as a supercritical branching process, meaning that a containment breach involving just a few viable cells effectively guarantees ecological establishment. Applying a non-ergodic rejection framework—where expected-value reasoning is inapplicable to states on which the biosphere's value functional vanishes—we show that the long-run probability of containment failure cannot be retired, rendering the admissible set of terrestrial research configurations mathematically empty. The paper also characterizes the strict physical and logistical conditions necessary for extraterrestrial research configurations to minimize residual risk, while explicitly stating that characterizing this boundary is not an endorsement of operating at it. Ultimately, the analysis demonstrates that the null configuration—not conducting the program—remains the unique research setup with zero residual risk.

detail.abstract: This paper documents the deep and wide-ranging impacts of depression across affected individuals and households. Using a stacked difference-indifferences event study design on 30 years of rich household longitudinal data, I show that the onset of an episode of clinical depression causes large and persistent falls in employment, hours, and earnings (even for those who remain employed), accompanied by falls in consumption, savings, and rates of homeownership that highlight incomplete insurance. Contrary to the standard added-worker effect, I find spousal employment and market income fall, as partners are shown to take up the role of care-giver, this coincides with higher divorce risk and worse average mental health in the rest of the household. A depressive episode is not simply an income shock for the directly affected household member, but a shock which closes the household's usual co-insurance margin between household members and imposes substantial costs.

detail.abstract: Intellectual Property Rights (IPR) constitute a fundamental component of modern legal, economic, technological, and cultural systems. They establish legal mechanisms for protecting creations of the human intellect, including literary and artistic works, inventions, industrial designs, trademarks, geographical indications, plant varieties, and commercially valuable confidential information. However, intellectual property cannot be understood as a single, uniform category of rights. It comprises several distinct legal regimes, each designed to address particular forms of intellectual creation, commercial interests, and public policy objectives [1-3]. This paper examines the comprehensive classification of intellectual property, distinguishing between copyright and related rights, industrial property, plant variety protection, trade secrets, traditional knowledge, traditional cultural expressions, and specialised forms of protection relevant to the digital economy. It analyses the principal categories recognised within India's intellectual property framework, including patents, trademarks, industrial designs, copyright, geographical indications, semiconductor integrated circuit layout-designs, plant varieties, and confidential commercial information. It also examines the relationship between intellectual property protection, innovation, economic development, cultural preservation, and public interest. Drawing upon Indian legislation, international agreements, authoritative institutional publications, and selected judicial decisions, the paper explains how different intellectual property rights may coexist in a single product or commercial activity. Particular attention is given to the distinction between legally recognised intellectual property rights and related protective mechanisms, such as domain-name dispute resolution, passing off, and defensive documentation of traditional knowledge. The paper concludes that a comprehensive classification of IPR requires an understanding of the subject matter, ownership, scope, duration, limitations, and enforcement mechanisms associated with each category.

detail.abstract: Debt is a game. A bilateral game is what turns debt into a trade or an exchange, and that much is settled; it is where economics does its work. This paper argues that an epistemic act lies beneath the game, an inference about collateral that debt involves in a way equity does not, and that price is representational signage on top of both. Price does not represent the asset or its value, and it is vague rather than unknown. The paper starts from the pawn-shop loan in Holmström (2015): the lender lends against a judgement that the object is good enough, and collateral obviates the need to discover its exact price. The "no questions asked" state that Holmström describes in money markets is read as the case in which the game goes on and nobody looks past the price. The lender's judgement, and a change in the rule that produces it, are given a formal statement. Disclosure is then treated as a sign that works on the epistemic layer: it can add information, change the rule, or leave readers who used to agree reading it differently. A disclosure also has an author, and a final section asks when an author who knows the market's reading rule will steer against it, and what changes when a steer is caught.

detail.abstract: Investment funds differ in how investors can access their capital. The redemption rules governing how and when investors can withdraw have evolved endogenously in response to shifting investor demand and regulatory constraints. While the immediate liquidity of open-end mutual funds and exchange-traded funds has long dominated the retail market, the landscape has been evolving over time.

title: The Russian Power Transmission Matrix Resource Transfusion and Inherited Mechanics of Command

detail.title: The Russian Power Transmission Matrix Resource Transfusion and Inherited Mechanics of Command

declarations.declarationOfInterest: none

detail.abstract: How do resources become usable political power when authority is concentrated, contested, or transferred? This article develops the Russian Power Transmission Matrix as a task-specific framework separating resource stocks, transfers between holders, access to deployment, and the mechanics converting deployment into effects. Its central proposition is that formal succession and resource acquisition do not automatically convey operational command. Inherited apparatuses can survive a change of authority while access to them changes; central accumulation can also coexist with systemic attrition. Conditional analytical results specify conservation for typed resources, jointly constrained deployment, and the effect of expanded access on attainable outcomes. Documents concerning early Soviet authority and collectivization supply bounded probes of contested execution and reporting. Post-Soviet scholarship identifies applications in fiscal redistribution, gubernatorial appointments, and regional resilience. These materials establish relevant mechanism fragments rather than a calibrated national matrix or uninterrupted historical lineage. The research design requires pre-outcome measurement, matched records, and comparison with resource-only and formal-authority explanations. The contribution is an independently testable decomposition of power transmission, with psychological persistence and resonance reserved for useparately identified extensions.

title: Ransomware in the Temple of Justice: Judicial Cybersecurity, Institutional Independence and the Integrity of Digital Court Records in Africa

detail.title: Ransomware in the Temple of Justice: Judicial Cybersecurity, Institutional Independence and the Integrity of Digital Court Records in Africa

declarations.ethicsApproval: This article is a doctrinal and comparative legal study based on publicly available sources, including court decisions, legislation and practice directions, official statements by judicial and executive bodies, an institutional survey report, and contemporaneous news reporting. All sources are attributed, and claims attributed to unnamed sources in news reporting are treated as allegations rather than findings, consistent with the methodological limitations set out in Part 2 of the article.

detail.abstract: The digital transformation of African judiciaries promises greater efficiency, transparency and access to justice, but it also creates institutional vulnerabilities whose consequences extend beyond the loss of information technology services. When electronic court systems are disrupted, the consequences may include inaccessible case files, delayed criminal proceedings, compromised evidence, missed procedural deadlines and threats to the confidentiality of judicial records. Where interference coincides with politically consequential proceedings, the integrity of judicial administration may also become a question of constitutional governance, although the motive and attribution of any particular incident must be established through evidence. This article examines judicial cyber-resilience through a comparative legal study of Kenya, Uganda and Nigeria, with South Africa's confirmed 2021 ransomware incident used as a benchmark. Kenya's July 2025 disruption of judicial digital services is a contemporary case study of the operational consequences of reported external interference. Uganda's emerging jurisprudence on electronically authenticated court process shows how judicial doctrine is adapting to digital records, while stakeholder evidence on the readiness of the Electronic Court Case Management Information System (ECCMIS) raises questions about training, accessibility and institutional preparedness. Nigeria's experience after the destruction of the Igbosere Court building shows that digital preservation is essential to judicial continuity even when disruption results from physical destruction rather than cyberattack. The article argues that criminalising unauthorised access, data interference and cyber extortion is necessary but insufficient. Effective judicial cyber-resilience also requires reliable backups, legally defensible record-restoration procedures, evidentiary authentication, continuity arrangements, procedural remedies and safeguards against interference with judicial independence. It proposes a Judicial Cyber-Resilience Framework integrating technical security with constitutional obligations, professional accountability and equitable access to justice, while distinguishing verified incidents from allegations concerning attribution or motive.

title: Post-sovereign Intelligence: Toward a Non-Anthropocentric Philosophy of Coexistence

detail.title: Post-sovereign Intelligence: Toward a Non-Anthropocentric Philosophy of Coexistence

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author developed the frameworks presented here and has an interest in their reception, including that of the forthcoming books in which related frameworks are developed. Readers should weight the paper's self-assessments accordingly.
